unit.title: Your team's story
unit.summary: Personalised: your team's identity, history, car and drivers, and how their fans talk.

lessons.title: {{team}}: who they are
lessons.objective: Say what {{team}} is known for, in one honest sentence.

payload.prompt: What makes {{team}} a constructor in Formula 1?

options.text: They build their own power unit and race in the sport.
options.explanation: Correct. Ferrari, Mercedes, and Audi design and build their own engines.

options.text: They buy engines from someone else and just race.
options.explanation: That makes them a customer team, not a constructor. McLaren buys from Mercedes.

options.text: They own an F1 team.
options.explanation: Ownership is not the same as being a constructor. A constructor builds the car and engine.

options.text: They have the fastest car.
options.explanation: Speed does not make you a constructor. {{team}} is defined by who builds the power unit.

explanation.correct: Right. A constructor builds its own power unit and competes in the championship.
explanation.incorrect: A constructor in F1 designs and builds its own power unit, or is owned by the engine maker.
explanation.sayThisLine: {{team}} is a constructor—they build their own engine.

payload.prompt: In one word, what is {{team}} known for in Formula 1?

options.text: Passion. {{team}} fans are the most vocal in the paddock.
options.explanation: Ferrari has the most legendary fans, the tifosi. But this is about what the team itself is known for.

options.text: Heritage. {{team}} has history and iconic moments that define the sport.
options.explanation: Yes. {{team}}'s story is tied to Formula 1's legend. Success and heartbreak have shaped them.

options.text: Technology. {{team}} has the most advanced power unit.
options.explanation: Engine performance varies year to year. {{team}}'s identity goes deeper than one era.

options.text: Reliability. {{team}} finishes every race without problems.
options.explanation: Reliability is a performance metric, not what defines {{team}}'s identity in the sport.

explanation.correct: Right. {{team}}'s legacy and heritage define them. Wins, losses, and turning points are part of who they are.
explanation.incorrect: {{team}} is known for their history in the sport. They are defined by their heritage and the moments that made them.
explanation.sayThisLine: {{team}} has a story that matters in F1.

payload.prompt: Is {{team}} a works team or a customer team in 2026?

options.text: Works: they design and build the Ferrari power unit.
options.explanation: Right. Ferrari is a works team. They own and develop their own engine.

options.text: Customer: they buy the Ferrari power unit from another builder.
options.explanation: Wrong. Ferrari builds their own. Haas and Cadillac are Ferrari customers.

options.text: Works: they design and build the Mercedes power unit.
options.explanation: Right. Mercedes is a works team on their own power unit.

options.text: Customer: {{team}} does not build its own power unit.
options.explanation: Wrong for this question. Check which team you are learning about.

explanation.correct: Right. {{team}} is a works team. They design the power unit themselves.
explanation.incorrect: {{team}} is a works team in 2026. They own and develop their power unit, not buy it from someone else.

statement.speaker: Someone at a watch party
statement.text: Who is {{team}}? Give an honest one-sentence answer.

options.text: {{team}} is a team with a long history in Formula 1, competing for championships every year.
options.explanation: Good. You named them and their role. Honest and clear.

options.text: {{team}} builds their own power unit and has fans all over the world.
options.explanation: Perfect. You said what they do. That is genuine engagement.

options.text: {{team}} is the best team and will definitely win the championship.
options.explanation: That sounds like blind fandom. Be honest, not promotional.

payload.translation: You are sharing what you honestly understand about {{team}}'s role and history in F1.

followUps.line: What makes {{team}} special to you?
followUps.why: You opened a door. Now listen to what matters to her about {{team}}.

followUps.line: Have they always been competitive, or are they rebuilding now?
followUps.why: This shows you are thinking about their current form and trajectory.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You are not supposed to know all the stats. Say what you understand, then ask her what makes {{team}} special.

lessons.title: {{team}}: eras and rivalries
lessons.objective: Place {{team}}'s peaks and slumps and who they fight.

payload.prompt: How would you describe {{team}}'s recent form heading into 2026?

options.text: Dominant: they have been winning championships regularly.
options.explanation: Check the 2024-2025 seasons. {{team}} had ups and downs, not continuous dominance.

options.text: Competitive: they fight for championships but do not always win.
options.explanation: Yes. {{team}} is always competitive but has had seasons of struggle and seasons of success.

options.text: Struggling: they are near the back of the grid.
options.explanation: {{team}} is not a back-marker. They compete at the front, even in tough years.

options.text: Improving: they were bad but are getting better now.
options.explanation: That is not quite right. {{team}}'s form is more complex than a steady climb.

explanation.correct: Right. {{team}} is competitive. They have winning years and rebuilding years, like all top teams.
explanation.incorrect: {{team}} fights at the front of the grid. Success is not automatic; they have to earn it.
explanation.sayThisLine: {{team}} is always competitive. Some years they win; some years they fight back.

payload.prompt: What is a regulation era in Formula 1?

options.text: A season where a team wins a lot of races.
options.explanation: That is a winning season, not an era. An era is longer.

options.text: A multi-year rulebook where car design stays similar, then resets.
options.explanation: Right. A new era changes the rules and who can compete. 2026 starts a new era.

options.text: The period when one driver wins many titles.
options.explanation: That is a driver's peak, not a regulation era. An era is about the cars and rules.

options.text: When a team dominates for several years.
options.explanation: Dominance can happen in an era, but the era is about the regulations, not the winning.

explanation.correct: Right. A regulation era is a rulebook cycle. Every few years, F1 changes the rules; the grid resets.
explanation.incorrect: An era is defined by the car regulations and rules, not by who is winning. A new era means new physics.
explanation.sayThisLine: Each era resets who can compete fairly.

payload.prompt: Who is {{team}}'s biggest rival in the championship?

options.text: The team with the fastest car each year.
options.explanation: Competitors change based on form. {{team}}'s rivals are teams that compete for the title.

options.text: Always the same team every year.
options.explanation: Rivalries shift. This year's competitor might be next year's ally, depending on form.

options.text: Whoever is competing for the championship with them that year.
options.explanation: Yes. {{team}}'s rivals are the teams that are close enough to fight for wins and points.

options.text: A team that {{team}} has disliked historically.
options.explanation: History matters, but real rivalry is about who is competing for points right now.

explanation.correct: Right. Rivals are not fixed. {{team}}'s competitors depend on who is fast that year.
explanation.incorrect: {{team}}'s rivals are the teams close enough to fight for the title. Rivalries shift with performance.

statement.speaker: A fan
statement.text: {{team}} had glory days but they are in a slump now. What do you think?

options.text: {{team}} has had great years and tough years, like most teams do. That is just how F1 works.
options.explanation: Good. You acknowledged both sides without being defensive or dismissive.

options.text: {{team}}'s history is complex. They won big, but I am still learning their story.
options.explanation: Perfect. You are honest about not knowing everything.

options.text: {{team}} is done. They will never win again.
options.explanation: Too pessimistic and final. F1 has rule resets and new opportunities.

payload.translation: You are responding to criticism of {{team}} by being balanced and honest about cycles in F1.

followUps.line: What was their best era, in your view?
followUps.why: You are asking her to share what she loves about {{team}}'s history.

followUps.line: Do you think they can come back with the 2026 rules reset?
followUps.why: This shows you know that regulation eras can change the competitive picture.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to defend {{team}}. Acknowledge the ups and downs. Ask her why this era matters to her.

statement.speaker: A fan asking
statement.text: Will {{team}} win the championship this year? What do you think?

options.text: That depends on whether their power unit is reliable and they develop the car faster than rivals.
options.explanation: Good. You named the real factors: power and development speed. No empty predictions.

options.text: That depends on the competition. Mercedes and McLaren look strong too.
options.explanation: Excellent. You acknowledged the bigger picture, not just {{team}}.

options.text: Of course {{team}} will win. They are the best.
options.explanation: That is blind optimism, not analysis. Championships are not guaranteed.

payload.translation: You are giving an honest, realistic take on {{team}}'s championship chances based on real factors.

followUps.line: What does {{team}} need most: a better power unit or better car development?
followUps.why: This shows you are thinking about their specific challenges.

followUps.line: How do you think {{team}} will compare to their main rivals this year?
followUps.why: You are asking her perspective on the competitive landscape.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: It is okay to say 'I do not know' and name what you are learning. That is honest.

lessons.title: {{team}}'s car and power unit now
lessons.objective: Explain {{team}}'s 2026 power unit and what it means.

payload.prompt: A 2026 power unit is made of what two main parts?

options.text: An old V10 engine and an electrical battery.
options.explanation: Wrong. F1 uses a V6 turbo in 2026, not a V10.

options.text: A turbocharged V6 engine and an electrical motor (MGU-K).
options.explanation: Correct. About 50% power from each; the electrical system is key to 2026.

options.text: A pure electric motor; no combustion engine.
options.explanation: No. F1 in 2026 still uses a turbo engine. Fully electric is Formula E.

options.text: Two turbo engines running together.
options.explanation: Wrong. Each car has one turbo power unit, made of engine + electrical parts.

explanation.correct: Right. A 2026 power unit is 50% engine and 50% electrical. They work as one system.
explanation.incorrect: The 2026 power unit is a V6 turbo plus an electrical motor. They are equally important.
explanation.sayThisLine: 2026 power units are half engine, half electrical.

options.text: Ferrari supplies the power unit (Ferrari is a works team).
options.explanation: Correct. Ferrari designs and builds the engine for Ferrari, Haas, and Cadillac.

options.text: Mercedes supplies the power unit (Mercedes is a works team).
options.explanation: Correct. Mercedes builds for Mercedes, McLaren, Williams, and Alpine.

options.text: Red Bull Ford supplies the power unit.
options.explanation: Correct. Red Bull and Ford partnered for 2026. They supply Red Bull and Racing Bulls.

options.text: Honda supplies the power unit.
options.explanation: Correct. Honda works with Aston Martin for 2026.

explanation.correct: Right. {{team}} uses the power unit from their supplier. Check which one that is.
explanation.incorrect: {{team}} has a power unit supplier in 2026. It depends on the team—check your person's team.

payload.prompt: Why does the power unit supplier matter for {{team}}'s performance?

options.text: Because the power unit is about half the total performance.
options.explanation: Right. A good power unit gives the whole team an advantage in power and reliability.

options.text: Because {{team}} likes one supplier over another.
options.explanation: Preference is not the issue. Performance and reliability are what count.

options.text: Because {{team}} pays more if the supplier is expensive.
options.explanation: Cost is a factor, but performance is what matters on the track.

options.text: It does not matter; the chassis is everything.
options.explanation: Wrong. Power unit is roughly equal to chassis in modern F1.

explanation.correct: Right. The power unit is half the performance. A strong supplier helps {{team}} compete.
explanation.incorrect: {{team}}'s power unit is a huge part of the car's performance. The supplier is critical.
explanation.sayThisLine: Power unit is half the battle in F1.

payload.prompt: Match each term to what it means.

pairs.definition: The turbo engine and electrical system together.
Extra upgrade chances for power makers that fall behind mid-season.
Freezing engine specs so teams cannot change them mid-season.
100% advanced fuel from biomass or waste, not petroleum.

explanation.summary: Good. You matched the power-unit terms. The power unit has an engine and electrical system; ADUO helps manufacturers stay competitive by offering mid-season upgrades.
explanation.sayThisLine: Power unit means engine and electrical together in modern F1.

lessons.title: {{driver}} and {{team}}'s line-up
lessons.objective: Know your person's driver, their teammate and the story between them.

payload.prompt: Why is the teammate the fairest test of a driver's skill?

options.text: Because they drive the same car, same engineer, same strategy.
options.explanation: Right. Everything is equal except the driver's talent and decisions.

options.text: Because they are always faster than the opposition.
options.explanation: Not always. But they are the closest you can get to a true comparison.

options.text: Because they get the better pit stops.
options.explanation: Pit stops are part of team strategy, but the teammate comparison is more subtle than one factor.

options.text: Because they are hired to help the lead driver.
options.explanation: Team orders happen, but the teammate battle reveals who is quicker one-on-one.

explanation.correct: Right. Same car means no excuses. The teammate battle is the best measure of driver quality.
explanation.incorrect: A teammate has the same car and setup. How a driver compares to them shows true performance.

payload.prompt: What does it mean if {{driver}} is out-qualified by their teammate?

options.text: {{driver}} is not as quick as their teammate in one-lap pace.
options.explanation: Right. Qualifying is one lap. It shows who is faster over a single push.

options.text: {{driver}} has a worse car setup.
options.explanation: Possibly, but both drivers usually have equal setup choices.

options.text: {{driver}} is slower at everything, not just qualifying.
options.explanation: No. One-lap pace and race pace are different. A driver can be slow in qualifying but strong in races.

options.text: {{driver}} did not push hard.
options.explanation: Could be, but drivers usually push in qualifying. It is more likely the teammate was faster.

explanation.correct: Right. Qualifying is one-lap pace. {{driver}} was slower than their teammate that day, over one lap.
explanation.incorrect: Qualifying measures one-lap pace only. {{driver}} was out-qualified on that metric.
explanation.sayThisLine: Qualifying is one lap; it does not define the whole season.

payload.prompt: What is a team order in Formula 1?

options.text: An instruction to one driver to let the other pass or hold station.
options.explanation: Right. Team orders are used for strategy or to help the leading driver.

options.text: A rule that says one driver is the team's favourite.
options.explanation: Team favour exists, but that is not what team orders are.

options.text: A penalty given for not following the team's strategy.
options.explanation: No. Team orders are a directive, not a punishment.

options.text: A rule that both drivers must fight equally.
options.explanation: That would be the opposite of team orders. Orders prioritise the team's goals.

explanation.correct: Right. Team orders are used to help the team win. One driver is asked to support the other.
explanation.incorrect: Team orders are instructions. A driver is told to let their teammate through or hold a position.
explanation.sayThisLine: Team orders put the team's title ahead of individual rivalry.

statement.speaker: Someone asking
statement.text: Is {{driver}} a good driver? What is your take on him?

options.text: {{driver}} is competitive with their teammate, which is a sign of real pace.
options.explanation: Good. You used the teammate benchmark, which is the fairest test.

options.text: {{driver}} has had good races and tough races, like most drivers do.
options.explanation: Perfect. You are balanced; no driver is flawless.

options.text: {{driver}} is the most talented driver ever.
options.explanation: That is overblown fandom. Let the results speak for themselves.

payload.translation: You are giving an honest assessment of {{driver}} based on what you have observed.

followUps.line: What makes you like {{driver}} in particular?
followUps.why: You listen to what she values in him before making your own judgments.

followUps.line: How does {{driver}} compare to their former teammates?
followUps.why: This shows you think about driver comparisons beyond just one season.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need a full resume. Just say what you have seen. Ask her what draws her to {{driver}}.

statement.speaker: A fan
statement.text: {{driver}}'s teammate is faster. It is frustrating. How do you see it?

options.text: That is tough. The teammate battle shows where the real pace difference lies.
options.explanation: Good. You acknowledged it and showed you understand its importance.

options.text: Maybe this season, but let us see how the rest of the year goes.
options.explanation: Perfect. You are balanced; seasons evolve and drivers adapt.

options.text: That must mean {{driver}} is not actually that good.
options.explanation: One season or one-lap pace does not define a driver's whole career.

payload.translation: You are responding with honesty about the teammate benchmark without being defensive.

followUps.line: Do you think {{driver}} can catch up, or is the teammate just stronger?
followUps.why: You are asking her to think deeper about the reasons, not just the result.

followUps.line: What would help {{driver}} close the gap?
followUps.why: This shows you think about solutions, not just complaints.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: It is okay to acknowledge if her driver is not out-performing the teammate. Ask about the reasons, not just the result.

lessons.title: How {{team}} fans talk
lessons.objective: Recognise fan in-jokes and pet peeves without faking it.

statement.speaker: Someone
statement.text: I am a {{team}} fan. What do you think about our fans?

options.text: {{team}} fans are passionate and stick with your team through tough times and good.
options.explanation: Good. You named something real about fan loyalty without stereotyping.

options.text: {{team}} fans have a lot of history and pride tied to your team's legacy.
options.explanation: Perfect. You acknowledged their perspective and shared history.

options.text: {{team}} fans are all crazy and loud at the races.
options.explanation: Stereotypes do not respect what fan culture actually means to people.

payload.translation: You are respectfully recognizing what makes {{team}} fans distinctive without stereotyping.

followUps.line: What makes you a {{team}} fan? How long have you been following them?
followUps.why: You are asking her to share her story, which opens real conversation.

followUps.line: What is the best moment you have had as a {{team}} fan?
followUps.why: This invites her to share joy, not just frustration.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to be a {{team}} fan yourself. Just be respectful of why they are.

statement.speaker: Race radio you overhear
statement.text: {{driver}}, box box this lap, tyres and fuel. What do you say to the person next to you?

options.text: The team just told {{driver}} to pit now for fresh tyres this lap.
options.explanation: Perfect. You translated race radio correctly. That is the skill.

options.text: {{driver}} is coming in for a pit stop. The team chose this specific lap.
options.explanation: Excellent. You showed you understand strategy timing matters.

options.text: I have no idea what that means.
options.explanation: Learning radio shorthand is part of belonging in F1 conversation.

payload.translation: You have decoded the radio message and explained what the pit call means.

followUps.line: Do you think this is the right time for {{driver}} to pit strategically?
followUps.why: You are asking whether the pit call makes strategic sense.

followUps.line: What other radio terms do you hear that confuse you?
followUps.why: Asking keeps you learning and honest about what you don't know yet.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Radio shorthand is a language fans learn. Learning to decode it is part of understanding F1 conversation.

statement.speaker: A fan
statement.text: {{driver}}'s contract is up in 2027. Silly season is starting. What does that mean?

options.text: So other teams are probably already thinking about signing him and building their line-ups.
options.explanation: Right. You linked contract expiry to driver-market speculation and seat movements.

options.text: That is when the paddock starts talking about who drives where next year.
options.explanation: Perfect. You know silly season is when seat moves and rumors peak.

options.text: Nothing special. Drivers always have contracts.
options.explanation: Contract expiry triggers silly season rumours. It is a big deal for market movement.

payload.translation: You understand that contract expiry triggers silly season speculation and driver-market activity.

followUps.line: Do you think {{driver}} should stay at {{team}} or move?
followUps.why: You are asking her thoughts on his career direction.

followUps.line: Which teams might be interested in signing him?
followUps.why: This keeps you engaged in the speculation without making up rumors.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Silly season speculation is fun but not certain. Acknowledge the rumor and ask what she thinks.

payload.title: {{team}} fan lingo
payload.setting: Chatting about {{team}}'s season after a race.

exchanges.theirMessage: That strategy call was awful. Box box way too late.

replies.text: So they missed the window? What would have helped?
replies.theirResponse: Earlier, before the traffic. They left him out too long.
replies.coachNote: You asked what the problem was. That shows you are following the strategy.
True, but you did not ask for details. Ask what went wrong.

replies.text: Pit stops only take two seconds anyway.
replies.theirResponse: That is not the point. Timing matters.
replies.coachNote: Pit time is short, but pit windows and traffic strategy are everything.

payload.closingNote: {{team}} fans talk strategy in detail. Listen for their frustration with pit calls and timing.

lessons.title: Good questions to ask a {{team}} fan
lessons.objective: Ask three follow-ups that show you have been listening.

statement.speaker: A {{team}} fan
statement.text: I am so upset about today's race. The strategy was terrible and we lost.

options.text: Do you think the strategy was wrong, or did the other team just have a faster car?
options.explanation: Excellent. You asked them to separate strategy from car performance.

options.text: What would {{team}} have needed to do differently to win the race?
options.explanation: Perfect. You turned frustration into analysis. That bonds fans.

options.text: Yeah, that strategy call was obviously wrong.
options.explanation: Pile-on agreement does not show you are really thinking. Ask her to explain.

payload.translation: You are asking thoughtful questions that turn frustration into strategic analysis.

followUps.line: What do you think the strategy team should have done instead?
followUps.why: You are asking her to think through the alternative, showing genuine curiosity.

followUps.line: Do you think this one race changes the championship outlook?
followUps.why: This keeps perspective and moves beyond one emotional moment.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Good questions turn complaints into conversations. Ask her to explain her view, not yours.

statement.speaker: A {{team}} fan
statement.text: I am really optimistic about next season. I think {{team}} can challenge for the title.

options.text: What upgrades is {{team}} bringing to the car this off-season?
options.explanation: Good. You asked about concrete preparation, which is what the fan cares about.

options.text: Do you think {{team}} can compete with the top teams on power-unit performance?
options.explanation: Perfect. You linked optimism to a real challenge: power-unit competitiveness matters.

options.text: Yeah, that sounds great!
options.explanation: Empty agreement does not show engagement. Ask what makes her optimistic.

payload.translation: You are asking informed questions about {{team}}'s preparations, not just cheering.

followUps.line: What do you think {{team}} needs most: a better power unit or better car development?
followUps.why: You are helping her think through specific challenges.

followUps.line: Who do you think will be {{team}}'s main rival for the title next year?
followUps.why: This keeps the conversation on real competitive dynamics.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Fans want to talk about what is coming. Ask about upgrades, rules or driver changes.

payload.title: Talking about {{team}} change
payload.setting: Discussing {{team}}'s recent technical or personnel moves.

exchanges.theirMessage: {{team}} just hired a new race engineer. I am nervous about it.

replies.text: What was the old engineer like? Why do you trust them more?
replies.theirResponse: He knew the car inside out. This new person has a lot to learn.
replies.coachNote: You asked her to explain her concern. That is respect.
Agree, but go deeper. Ask why she is worried.

replies.text: New people bring fresh ideas. It will be better.
replies.theirResponse: You do not know that. You do not follow {{team}}.
replies.coachNote: Dismissing her knowledge backfires. Listen first; then offer perspective.

exchanges.theirMessage: But maybe {{team}} needed a change. The car development was slow.

replies.text: So the old engineer was part of the problem?
replies.theirResponse: Maybe. Or maybe {{team}} just did not give him the resources he needed.
replies.coachNote: You let her work through it. That is the real skill.
Agree, but keep asking. She is thinking it through.

replies.text: Yeah, they have been bad for years.
replies.coachNote: Pile-on criticism does not help. Stick to what you know.

payload.closingNote: {{team}} fans have strong feelings about team changes. Listen to their history with the team.

payload.title: Finding common ground
payload.setting: A {{team}} fan is passionate. You want to connect.

exchanges.theirMessage: I love {{team}}, but they break my heart sometimes.

replies.text: That is the price of caring, right? What moment hurt the most?
replies.theirResponse: Oh, so many. But I am still here.
replies.coachNote: You validated her feelings and asked her story. Perfect.
You do not have to have lived her heartbreak. Ask her to explain it.

replies.text: Why not just pick a winning team?
replies.theirResponse: That is not how it works.
replies.coachNote: Fandom is not rational. Respect that, even if it seems strange to you.

payload.closingNote: {{team}} loyalty is earned and tested. Listen to why they stay despite the pain.
